editorial.focus: This puzzle stays in the tool shed: digging, carrying, watering, and keeping plants supported. The answers name tools and supplies rather than flowers or vegetables, so each clue gives you a specific garden job to picture.
editorial.solvingTip: Look for the job in the clue. A tool for lifting soil is different from one for gathering leaves. At a crossing, check both words before changing a letter that already fits.

answerNotes.text: A spade is typically associated with a flat blade and straight cutting edge. A shovel generally has a more scooped blade, although everyday names for the two can overlap.
A stake is a support post, not the string used to fasten a plant to it. The clue asks for the post itself.
A watering can is a portable container with a spout. The fill-in-the-blank clue supplies 'watering' so the short answer is the container's name.

editorial.solvingTip: Look for the distinguishing detail: honey, a shell, a web, or a long pair of ears. A clue about something an animal builds asks for the object, not the animal that made it.

answerNotes.text: Ladybug is the familiar American name for this beetle; ladybird is common in British English. Many ladybugs feed on aphids, making them welcome garden visitors.
Spiders have eight legs and are arachnids, not insects. Insects such as ants and bees have six legs, a distinction that makes this clue specific.
The coiled shell helps distinguish a snail from a slug. Both can turn up among garden plants.

editorial.focus: The answers follow the early stages of growing a plant: containers, moisture, planting depth, and new growth. The clues explain their context directly. This is a vocabulary puzzle, not a planting calendar; the right conditions depend on the seed being grown.
editorial.solvingTip: Think about what happens above and below the soil. A root grows downward, while a shoot develops upward. Action clues such as 'Plant seeds in soil' call for a verb rather than the name of a tool.

answerNotes.text: Planting depth describes how far below the surface a seed is placed. Seed packets give different recommendations, so there is no single depth for every crop.
In gardening, thin can be a verb meaning to remove some seedlings so others have more room. It does not refer to the shape of a seedling here.
A root takes up water and anchors the plant. A shoot is the young upward-growing part, so the direction described in a clue helps you choose between them.
